UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Midcontinent Independent System                )                   Docket No. ER26-3650-000
      Operator, Inc.                           )


                  LIMITED PROTEST OF ENTERGY SERVICES, LLC

       Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §

385.211, Entergy Services, LLC (“Entergy Services”), on behalf of the Entergy Operating

Companies (Entergy Arkansas, LLC, Entergy Louisiana, LLC, Entergy Mississippi, LLC,

Entergy New Orleans, LLC, and Entergy Texas, Inc.) (collectively, “Entergy”), files this Limited

Protest in response to the August 28, 2026, filing of the Midcontinent Independent System

Operator, Inc. (“MISO”). In that filing, MISO proposes to revise its Open Access Transmission,

Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) to establish interconnection reliability

requirements for Large Loads (the “Filing”).

       Entergy supports adoption of requirements meant to ensure that Large Loads are reliably

integrated into the bulk electric system. Indeed, Entergy has made significant and good faith

efforts to work with MISO to identify reliability requirements for Large Loads. Entergy is filing

this Limited Protest because, for certain reliability requirements, MISO proposes to include only

generalized requirements in the Tariff, while relegating the operative technical requirements and

key numeric thresholds to an unfiled Business Practice Manual (“BPM”). Specifically, for Large

Load forecast data requirements, Phasor Measurement Unit (“PMU”) requirements, Large Load

ride-through requirements, and Large Load ramp requirements, MISO improperly proposes to

include in a BPM the specific requirements that a Transmission Customer serving a Large Load

will be required to meet. Under the Commission’s “rule of reason” test, those requirements must
 be included in the Tariff. The Commission thus should condition any acceptance of MISO’s

filing on a compliance filing as described in Part II.C below. The Commission also should defer

the effective date of the Tariff provisions in the Filing until the compliance filing is accepted.

I.     BACKGROUND

       The Filing is one of a series MISO is making in response to the Commission’s June 18,

2026, order instituting a proceeding under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act, directing MISO

to show cause why its Tariff should not be found unjust and unreasonable for failing to

adequately address the interconnection and reliable operation of Large Loads.1 The Commission

granted MISO a 90-day abeyance to develop its response through the stakeholder process.2

       In the Filing, MISO proposes to add a new Module B, Section 37A to the Tariff,

establishing interconnection reliability requirements for Large Loads. New definitions are also

set forth for “Large Load” (defined as load with demand of 50 MW or more at a single

substation) and “Computational Load” (defined as a Large Load of 25 MW or more of

information-technology demand, such as data centers).3 At the center of this Limited Protest are

MISO’s proposed new categories of interconnection reliability requirements in the proposed new

Module. Those categories include Large Load forecast data requirements, PMU requirements,

Large Load ride-through requirements, and Large Load ramp requirements. While MISO has

filed generic Tariff language mandating compliance, key provisions of the forecast data

requirements, PMU requirements, ride-through requirements, and ramp requirements are

completely absent from the filing and according to MISO, will be contained in BPMs that in

II.     LIMITED PROTEST

       At the outset, Entergy emphasizes that it supports transparent reliability requirements for

Large Loads. Entergy also supports the ongoing efforts of the North American Electric

Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) to develop reliability standards for Large Loads under its

authority as the nation’s Electric Reliability Organization. Importantly, NERC’s process will

result in standards that will apply uniformly across the country. As the Commission recognized

in the Show Cause Order, large customer projects take significant resources to develop.4

Ensuring compliance with reliability requirements is a complex, technical process that may

involve significant capital expenditure depending on the data center design. Yet, to date, MISO’s

proposed Tariff language lacks essential technical and operational requirements. The undrafted

BPMs will contain critical details on the specific requirements and how compliance can be

achieved. Without this transparency, Transmission Customers and Large Loads cannot

meaningfully understand the obligations the Tariff would impose, nor evaluate their operational

or financial impact.

        A.        The Rule of Reason Test

       Section 205(c) of the Federal Power Act requires a public utility to file not only its rates,

but the practices affecting those rates.5 When determining whether a practice affecting rates

must be included in a tariff or may be included in a BPM, the Commission applies a “rule of

reason” standard.6 Under that standard, a tariff must include all practices that: (a) “significantly

affect rates, terms, and conditions of service,” (b) are “readily susceptible of specification,” and

(c) “are not so generally understood in any contractual arrangement as to render recitation

superfluous.”7

       On the other hand, “items better classified as implementation details” may be included in

a BPM.8 As the Commission has explained, “[i]t is appropriate for Business Practice Manuals to

contain implementation details, such as instructions, guidelines, examples and charts, which

guide internal operations and inform market participants of how [the RTO] conducts its

operations under [its Tariff].”9 The information contained in a BPM “is meant to provide further

explanation of the [Transmission Provider’s] practices but not significantly affect any rates,

        B.       MISO’s Filing Contravenes the Commission’s Rule of Reason that Requires
                 the Operative Reliability Requirements to be Stated in the Filed Tariff, Not
                 an Unfiled BPM

        At the time of this filing, MISO has only provided draft BPM language for disturbance

ride-through and operational forecasting. However, pending completion of BPMs, MISO has

proposed other reliability requirements in other presentations or statements. As Entergy will

explain, comparing MISO’s proposed Tariff language for Large Load forecast data requirements,

PMU requirements, Large Load ride-through requirements, and Large Load ramp requirements

to MISO’s draft BPM language or other recommendations makes clear that MISO’s filing fails

the rule of reason test for those requirements. MISO improperly proposes to include in a BPM

the specific requirements that a Transmission Customer serving a Large Load will be required to

meet.

       A measure to determine the substantive versus secondary impact of MISO’s proposed

forecasting requirements is to view them from the lens of potential cost of compliance. Whether

a Transmission Customer must maintain a rolling 168-hour hourly forecast updated hourly and a

rolling 6-hour, 5-minute forecast delivered at least 9 minutes ahead of each interval dictates the

metering equipment, associated software systems, and personnel staffing a Large Load must

procure to meet the requirement(s). Additionally, because MISO proposes to enforce the

forecasting requirements it sets forth through a cost-causation incentive that allocates make-

whole, commitment, balancing, congestion, and shortage-pricing charges commensurate with the

forecast error (under a formula MISO dictates),21 the forecast requirements directly determine the

charges a Transmission Customer serving a Large Load will pay. In short, MISO proposes to

convert forecast errors measured using its own criteria into costs charged to the Transmission

Customer through existing MISO settlement mechanisms.

        C.      The Commission Should Accept MISO’s Filing Subject to a Compliance
               Filing, With the Effective Date Deferred Until That Filing Is Accepted

       Entergy recognizes that MISO and its Transmission Owners are under a Commission

directive to address Large Load reliability, and Entergy shares the goal of reliable integration of

Large Loads. Entergy’s interest is in a Tariff it can read, comply with, and plan for costs needed

to implement it. Indeed, that is what is required under the rule of reason test. Core, statable, and

specific reliability requirements must be included in the filed Tariff.

       Consistent with the rule of reason and precedent,46 the Commission should direct MISO,

in a compliance filing, to include in the Tariff specific Large Load forecast data requirements,

   11.        Large Load Ride-Through Requirements
   11.1 Purpose
The purpose of the ride-through requirements is to reduce the risk of unnecessary
disconnection or rapid changes in Demand associated with Computational Load during voltage
and frequency disturbances and to support predictable disturbance performance during credible
Transmission System events.
As Computational Loads increasingly incorporate power-electronic interfaces, fast controls, and
dynamic operating behavior, their response to Transmission System disturbances may
materially affect system performance, operational reliability, and post-contingency recovery.
Ride-through requirements establish minimum performance expectations for maintaining
connection and stable operation during voltage and frequency disturbances and for recovering
active power following disturbance clearance.
Consistent with Section 37A.6 of the Tariff, Computational Load subject to this Section shall
remain connected to the Transmission System and continue operation during voltage and
frequency disturbances within the applicable performance criteria specified in this Section.
   11.2 General Ride-Through Requirements
Ride-through requirements shall apply at the applicable Point(s) of Withdrawal (“PoW(s)”) of a
Large Load and shall be evaluated based on voltage and frequency conditions measured at the
PoW(s).
When system conditions remain within the applicable ride-through performance limits specified
in Sections 11.3 and 11.4, the Computational Load shall remain connected to the Transmission
System and maintain stable operation.
Protection systems, converter protections, transfer schemes, facility controls, and other Large
Load Equipment shall be coordinated to avoid unnecessary tripping, interruption of service, or
unstable operation during disturbances within the applicable ride-through limits.
Following disturbance clearance, the Computational Load shall recover toward its pre-
disturbance operating condition in accordance with the applicable performance requirements of
this Section.


   11.3 Voltage Ride-Through Requirements
Computational Load shall remain connected to the Transmission System and maintain stable
operation during voltage disturbances when voltage measured at the applicable PoW(s)
remains within the voltage ride-through requirements specified in this Section.
Protection systems and facility controls shall be coordinated to avoid unnecessary
disconnection and to support stable operation during and following voltage disturbances.

    11.3.1 Voltage Ride-Through Envelope
Voltage ride-through performance shall be determined based on the root-mean-square voltage
magnitude measured at the applicable PoW(s) and the duration of the voltage excursion.

Computational Load shall remain connected to the Transmission System and avoid
unnecessary disconnection during short-duration transient overvoltage conditions associated

Protection systems, converter protections, and facility controls shall be coordinated to avoid
unnecessary interruption of service resulting from instantaneous or short-duration transient
voltage excursions that do not represent sustained abnormal system conditions. These
requirements are intended to support predictable disturbance performance and reduce the risk
of unnecessary changes in large load demand during credible transmission events.

unnecessary disconnection or unstable operation resulting from allowable phase angle changes

review and coordination, equipment or manufacturer documentation, control-setting verification,
or other supporting technical information acceptable to MISO.
The applicable dynamic models shall represent protection, control, disconnection, active power
reduction, and active power recovery behavior to the extent necessary to evaluate the
applicable ride-through performance requirements.
Where MISO determines that positive-sequence dynamic simulation is insufficient to evaluate
applicable ride-through behavior, MISO may require EMT analysis using the applicable EMT
models submitted pursuant to the modeling requirements of this BPM.

    11.5.2 Operational Performance Verification
MISO may verify actual ride-through performance using available operational and disturbance
data, including PMU data, SCADA data, disturbance monitoring records, event records, or other
relevant measurements associated with the applicable PoW(s).
Operational performance may be compared with the applicable ride-through requirements and
submitted models to support post-event analysis and model validation.
Detailed operational performance verification procedures will be established through a future
revision of this BPM.

   11.1 Purpose
   The purpose of this section is to establish the technical, operational, installation,
   communication, and naming requirements for phasor measurement units (PMUs) or
   equivalent synchronized measurement devices required for Computational Loads. These
   requirements ensure that high‑resolution, time‑synchronized phasor data is available to
   support real‑time situational awareness, oscillation detection, performance monitoring,
   including ride‑through requirement validation, after‑the‑fact event analysis, and dynamic
   model validation across the MISO footprint.
   This section defines the minimum functional capabilities, data quality criteria, measurement
   types, and streaming expectations necessary for PMUs installed at Points of Withdrawal,
   and outlines roles and responsibilities for ensuring compliance with Tariff §37A
   Interconnection Reliability Requirements. Together, these requirements provide a
   consistent, reliable standard for PMU observability of Computational Loads and ensure
   alignment with applicable IEEE/IEC synchrophasor measurement and communication
   standards.
   11.2 PMU Definition
   A phasor measurement unit (PMU) is a device which measures the electrical voltage and
   current waveforms on a power grid that are synchronized to a common time source. Time
   synchronization allows monitoring of synchronized real-time measurements of multiple
   remote measurement points on the grid. A PMU can be a dedicated device, or the PMU
   function can be incorporated into a protective relay, digital fault recorder (DFR), dynamic
   disturbance recorder (DDR), or other devices that can meet the below requirements and
   additional requirements specified in the later sections of this document.
   •     Measurements need to be synchronized with a high accuracy satellite clock (e.g.
         GPS/IRIG-B)
   •     Data needs to be recorded at least at 60 samples per second and support continuous
         streaming of data to MISO.
   •     The device must be capable of sampling and/or calculating all signals specified in 11.10
         meeting minimum accuracy limits defined in the standard IEC/IEEE 60255-118-1:2018
         for the P-Class PMU.

   11.3 Applicability and Scope
   PMU requirements defined in this section apply to all Computational Loads as defined under
   the MISO Tariff Interconnection Reliability Requirements. PMU-capable equipment must be
   installed prior to the later of the Service Commencement Date of the Computational Load, or
   September 1, 2027.
   Computational Loads are required to have PMU’s to support oscillation detection, wide area
   monitoring, performance monitoring including ride through requirement validation, after-the-
   fact event analysis and dynamic model validation.

   11.4 Installation Requirements
       For a Computational Load, the Transmission Owner (TO) is required to install PMU (as
   defined in Section 11.2) at each Point of Withdrawal (POW) on the Transmission Owner’s
   side of the POW. The PMU shall provide real-time data output to MISO and adhere to the
   standards listed below.

   •     IEEE/IEC 60255-118-1-2018 – Measurement requirements for synchrophasors,
         frequency and rate of change of frequency
   •     IEEE C37.118.2-2024 – Communication requirements for real-time communication
         between PMU’s, PDC and other applications
   •     Existing PMU’s shall comply to the earlier revisions of these standards including IEEE
         C37.118.1-2011 for measurement and IEEE C37.118.2-2011 for communication
   Use of a phasor data concentrator (PDC) on the TO side is preferred to consolidate multiple
   PMU streams into a single stream. This simplifies integration with MISO’s system and
   reduces connection complexity, eases data quality management.

   11.4.1 Hardware Requirements
   • PMU shall be set to have an output reporting rate of at least 60 samples per second
   • PMU shall have timing accuracy of 3µs
   • All data recorded will be in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)
   • PMU shall have GPS (UTC) synchronization function either through an internal or
       external GPS receiver
   • The PMU data stream shall indicate whether it is using GPS clock or local clock
   • GPS clock shall report time and time quality compatible to IEEE/IEC 60255-118-1-2018
   • Any intermediary PDC shall have GPS (UTC) synchronization function either through an
       internal or external GPS receiver

   11.4.2 Communication Requirements
   • Interface to PDC through private IP networks
   • Receive and send real-time data through TCP/UDP ports, user configurable (each port
       individually configurable).
   • Network communication between PMU and PDC is defined by Member
   • Latency from PMU to MISO PDC shall be no more than 0.50 seconds.

   118-1-2018 format at a sampling rate of 60 samples per second.

   11.7 Data Retention
   Current MISO data retention for synchrophasor data is as below:
   •     Full resolution for A, B and C phase data is retained for 6 months; and all other data is
         retained for 1 year.
   •     Down sampled data to one sample per second is retained for 2 years.
   •     MISO PMU data retention does not replace any local storage requirements including
         obligations that come from existing and future NERC standards.
   11.8 Required PMU Measurements
   PMU’s at the Computational Loads must be able to sample and/or calculate the following
   signals:

   11.8.1 Substation Measurements
   • Frequency - calculated from positive sequence voltage angle
   • Rate of Change of Frequency (ROCOF)
   • Quality

   11.8.2 Point of Withdrawal (POW) Measurements
   • Phase A: voltage magnitude and angle
   • Phase B: voltage magnitude and angle
   • Phase C: voltage magnitude and angle
   • Phase A: current magnitude and angle
   • Phase B: current magnitude and angle
   • Phase C: current magnitude and angle
   • Positive sequence for voltage magnitude and angle
   • Positive sequence for current magnitude and angle
   • Quality
